record_reviews.summary: Darwin reports the proposed uniform Zoology of the Beagle publication, asks Jenyns whether he would describe the fish, discusses funding, parts, artists, and specimens, and asks him to consult Henslow.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Single editorially supplied day, 10 April [1837], with no surviving uncertainty beyond the supplied year.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin writes the body; Maclay, Yarrell, Henslow and other zoologists are reported third parties, not additional voices.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: This outgoing proposal asks for Jenyns’s opinion, but no incoming Jenyns letter is in the packet to serve as its prompt.

evidence.quote: I should much like to know what you think about it
If you should happen to see Henslow in the course of a few day talk with him on the subject

record_reviews.summary: FitzRoy replies to a Darwin note received the previous evening, declines to advise on the wording of Darwin’s preface, and offers only a general commendation of Beagle officers.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: FitzRoy writes all retained paragraphs; Beaufort and Parry are named as people he consulted.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The antecedent Darwin note, dated Monday, is absent from the packet; the body does not answer any surviving outgoing record here.

evidence.quote: in answer to the note (dated Monday) received yesterday evening
decline giving any opinion—at present—upon the wording of a preface

record_reviews.summary: FitzRoy gives an extended, emotionally explicit critique of Darwin’s Beagle preface, says the officers deserve acknowledgment, answers three questions in a postscript, and offers to repair impressions with others.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Secure single day, 16 November 1837; the body itself refers to a letter written that morning and another letter of Monday, so multiple Darwin antecedents are possible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: FitzRoy writes the retained body; the quoted preface wording is Darwin’s external letter text, and Lyell’s conversation is FitzRoy’s report.

alternative_candidates_considered.assessment: Both concern the preface, but 387 says it answers a letter written that morning while 386 answers a Monday note received the prior evening; they are not treated as one letter chain.

record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The Darwin letter written that morning and the earlier Monday letter are not preserved in this packet; 386 is not used as 387’s antecedent.

evidence.quote: Your letter—written this morning—speaks the language of your own heart
The sentence by which I was specially struck in your letter of Monday last
Respecting your three questions

record_reviews.summary: Darwin encourages Jenyns’s fish work, offers fish drawings and lithography, discusses publication order and specimens, and reports that Henslow hears Jenyns groan over the fish.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin writes the body; Henslow’s report and the named voyages are cited context, not embedded correspondence.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The letter refers to Jenyns’s ongoing fish labour and Henslow’s oral report, but no surviving Jenyns incoming letter is assigned.

evidence.quote: Henslow tells me he hears a groan occasionally escape from you
I will have any or all the fish you think new lithographed

record_reviews.summary: Darwin answers Jenyns’s distress about the fish, reassures him about timing and number sizes, describes publication sequencing, and warns him not to continue if health or time makes the task unrewarding.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Single editorially supplied day, 4 December [1837], immediately after 391 but with a distinct incoming letter explicitly received that morning.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin writes all retained paragraphs; Eyton and the publisher are reported third parties.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The Jenyns letter received that morning is missing; the phrase about two Darwin letters concerns Darwin’s transmission, not a surviving prompt.

evidence.quote: before I received yours this morning
you must not for a moment hesitate about throwing it up

record_reviews.summary: FitzRoy answers matters about Richardson, Darwin’s volume and its printer copy, approves the work, says he will forward it to Captain Hall, and asks to hear where Whewell’s notice can be seen.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: FitzRoy writes the retained body; Richardson, Hall, Whewell and Earle are discussed as external people or works.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The Darwin request or communication about Richardson, the volume and Whewell’s speech is missing; no packet outgoing is a textual antecedent.

evidence.quote: Had I wished to look at it—I would have written but it is not in my line
I have sealed up the copy sent to me by your Printer and will forward it to Capt. B. Hall with King’s
If Mr. Whewell’s notice of your work is published

record_reviews.summary: FitzRoy argues that advertisements for Darwin’s Zoology and Geology should accompany the Beagle volumes, distinguishes ordinary advertisements from useful notices, and comments on plates, maps and the publisher’s review.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: FitzRoy writes the retained body; Colburn, Gardner and “B. H.” are reported third parties.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The Darwin communication or conversation to which this discussion responds is not preserved in the packet; shared publication context does not identify one.

evidence.quote: there is surely every reason for my wishing that an advertisement of the Zoology which you are bringing out
The Keeling Islands are reserved for one of your covering boards

record_reviews.summary: FitzRoy explains his absence, says he has only sampled Darwin’s volume and will read it in the country, promises a fuller letter, and mentions the Athenæum and a visit to the Darwins.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Alternative dates 2 or 16 June 1839 remain explicitly held; the Sunday morning body does not resolve them.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: FitzRoy writes the retained body; Mrs FitzRoy, the Darwins, Rice Trevor and the Athenæum are contextual references.

alternative_candidates_considered.assessment: 522 is later and mentions a communication about Mr Brown and continued book reading, but it does not prove that 516 is its antecedent; both can reflect missing Darwin communications.

record_reviews.unmatched_reason: No specific Darwin incoming text is preserved. FitzRoy’s promise to write after reading the volume points to a future response, not a prompt among the packet’s outgoing letters.

evidence.quote: I have not even yet read your volume
When I have read it through—I will write fully & freely to you on the subject

record_reviews.summary: FitzRoy thanks Darwin for a communication about Mr Brown, condemns Brown’s treatment of King’s plants, discusses Anderson’s public support, and says he is occupied with Darwin’s book.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: FitzRoy writes all retained paragraphs; Brown, King and Anderson are subjects of FitzRoy’s account, not additional letter voices.

alternative_candidates_considered.assessment: The earlier FitzRoy letter promises a later book discussion, but 522’s explicit Mr Brown communication and its distinct argument do not uniquely identify 516 as its antecedent.

record_reviews.unmatched_reason: Darwin’s communication respecting Mr Brown is absent; no outgoing Darwin letter in this packet contains that distinctive subject.

evidence.quote: Thank you for the communication respecting Mr. Brown
I am eagerly and most agreeably occupied with your book

record_reviews.summary: Darwin thanks Jenyns for his letter, discusses the Acant fish manuscript, illustrations, deadlines, meetings and his own geology, and reassures him that the difficult fish work will be worthwhile.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin writes the body; Henslow, Yarrell and Andrew Smith are reported third parties.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: Paragraph 1 explicitly answers Jenyns’s missing letter; no incoming Jenyns record is in this packet.

evidence.quote: thank you for your letter
I am really very sorry that you find my fish such a troublesome job

record_reviews.summary: Darwin responds to Jenyns’s progress with the fish, arranges Hawkins as artist, asks about sheets, plates and fish counts, answers eight specimen questions, and requests a prompt reply.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin writes all retained paragraphs; Yarrell, Hawkins and Richardson are third-party or technical context.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The Jenyns letter reporting progress and posing the questions is missing; the topical details cannot identify a surviving incoming record.

evidence.quote: I am delighted to hear that you are so forward
I will now answer your questions as far as lies in my power

record_reviews.summary: Darwin thanks Jenyns for a prompt answer, arranges five fish and more specimens for Hawkins, discusses timing, number price, manuscript length and a possible preface, and answers a locality question.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin writes the body; Hawkins, Yarrell and Syme are external people or references.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The prompt Jenyns answer is absent; the fact of a quick reply does not establish which unlocated letter or note supplied each point.

evidence.quote: Many thanks for your prompt answer
Shall you give a short preface

record_reviews.summary: Darwin says he missed the previous post, reassures Jenyns that he will not pay for the fish illustrations, agrees to discuss the selection, and reacts to the number of new genera.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Alternative dates 20 or 27 October 1839 remain held; the body’s “yesterday” does not select between them.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin writes the retained body; Jenyns’s reported selection and the technical work remain the subject of Darwin’s voice.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The Jenyns letter left unanswered by the prior post is missing; no packet incoming record is safely identified.

evidence.quote: your letter remains unanswered till tomorrows post
I am astonished & glad to hear how many new things you seem to have found

record_reviews.summary: Darwin answers FitzRoy’s long letter with news of health, Coral volume delays, sales, Whewell’s tides theory, naval promotion concerns, family life and enduring gratitude for the Beagle.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Single editorially supplied day, 20 February 1840, while the header prints Thursday 21st; the packet date constraint is retained.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin writes the body; FitzRoy, Whewell, Sulivan and Usborne are discussed as third parties or correspondents.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The “long letter” from FitzRoy is not among the packet records; the 1839 FitzRoy letters here are shorter and do not uniquely supply these subjects.

evidence.quote: I was very glad to receive your long letter
I think it far the most fortunate circumstance in my life that the chance afforded by your offer of taking a naturalist fell on me

record_reviews.summary: Darwin asks Jenyns whether his next fish number will be ready by June, explains publication delays caused by Owen and Darwin’s illness, and praises the already published fish number.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin writes all retained paragraphs; Owen and Henslow are named third parties.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: This is a planning request with no surviving Jenyns prompt in the packet; the earlier fish correspondence is context only.

evidence.quote: I have been intending for some time to write to you to ask some fishy questions
I hope you received your extra copies of the Fish

record_reviews.summary: Darwin answers a forwarded Jenyns note, promises to send the manuscript to the printer and consult Hawkins about the fish, and discusses his health and Easter-week meeting.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Single editorially supplied day, 5 April [1840]; the internal return window is 10–12 April.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin writes all retained paragraphs; Hawkins and Darwin’s father are contextual references.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The forwarded Jenyns note is absent. The response scope is identifiable as manuscript/fish logistics, but no surviving incoming letter can be linked.

evidence.quote: Your note has just been forwarded to me
I shall certainly be in Town by the end of next week, (ie 10th, or 11th, or 12th)

record_reviews.summary: Jenyns’s surviving text begins mid-sentence with a proposed Cambridge stay during lecturing, then breaks off; its postscript reports Lowe’s view that a Galápagos Scorpæna may match a Mediterranean and Atlantic species.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Circa 30 March 1841; the circa qualifier and missing opening remain unresolved.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Jenyns is the attributed writer, but the opening is a fragment and the missing text prevents confident reconstruction of the addressee or prompt.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: This incomplete incoming fragment does not uniquely answer any Darwin outgoing record in the packet; its health and Scorpæna remarks are not matched by 599.

evidence.quote: time of his lecturing at Cambridge
I had a letter the other day from Lowe of Madeira

record_reviews.summary: Darwin apologizes for delayed news of his health, responds to Jenyns’s health enquiries, tells him not to hurry the Fish part, and reports Bell’s incomplete work.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin writes the body; Doctors, Bell and Hitcham are reported context.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The Jenyns enquiries and earlier reassurance to which Darwin refers are not preserved; the 1841 fragment 596 has different surviving subject matter.

evidence.quote: answering your kind enquiries about me & mine
I can only repeat, what I have said before to beg you not to give yourself any anxiety

record_reviews.summary: Darwin acknowledges Jenyns’s note, negotiates five or six plates, sends Diodon notes for extraction and alteration, and reports his own limited health and meetings.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Bounded [November 1841] with no day resolved; the Wednesday header does not narrow the month.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin writes the retained body; Bell and the Journal are reported context, while the supplied Diodon notes are an enclosure/external text.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: Jenyns’s received note is missing; the Diodon material is an enclosure and cannot be substituted for the missing incoming letter.

evidence.quote: I was delighted to receive your note
You will find in my Journal p. 13 & 14 some account of the habits of the Diodon

record_reviews.summary: Darwin approves Jenyns’s introduction, sets out printer proof routing, promises to consult Hawkins about outlines, and expresses concern for Jenyns’s illness.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Questioned single-day date [13? January 1842]; the question mark remains and no body evidence resolves it.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin writes the body; the printer address and Hawkins are logistical context, not separate voices.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The introduction/manuscript and Jenyns illness report are not preserved as an incoming packet record; this outgoing response cannot be paired directly.

evidence.quote: I have read over your introduction & like it very much
How unfortunate it has been your unwellness this week

record_reviews.summary: Darwin answers Jenyns’s notes about White’s Selborne project and Furnarius, endorsing the separate work while criticizing G. R. Gray’s naming and invoking Strickland’s laws.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Bounded [May–September 1842]; the Wednesday header does not resolve a section day.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin writes the retained body; White, Gray and Strickland are external authors or works.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The Jenyns notes are absent. Their two topics are explicit, but no incoming record in the packet supplies the prompt.

evidence.quote: I am very glad to hear the notes to White are only the forerunner of a separate work
Your note on the Furnarius appears to me just the thing

record_reviews.summary: Darwin corrects a fish-number mistake, arranges immediate dispatch of fish skins and bottles, congratulates Jenyns on finishing the Fish, and mentions his Coral Reefs index and impending move.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin writes the retained body; Smith & Elder and Mr Crouch are logistical third parties.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The Jenyns communication about the fish-number mistake is missing; the publisher’s dispatch does not identify an incoming letter.

evidence.quote: I am sorry about the mistake of the Fish-numbers
You must feel lightened of no inconsiderable load, having finished the Fish

record_reviews.summary: Darwin reacts to a newspaper report of FitzRoy’s appointment as Governor of New Zealand, asks whether it is true and when FitzRoy sails, and requests a brief meeting before departure.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin writes the body; the newspaper appointment report and Mrs FitzRoy’s voyage are external context.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The direct stimulus is a newspaper report, not a surviving FitzRoy letter; no incoming packet record confirms or answers the appointment.

evidence.quote: I read yesterday with surprise and the greatest interest, your appointment as Governor of New Zealand
My object in writing is to beg of you or Mrs. FitzRoy to have the kindness to send me one line

issues: All 23 packet records were read in full: every retained body paragraph, header text, metadata date constraints/audit, editorial summary and editorial footnotes were inspected. The metadata flag has_transcription_in_preserved_xml:false was not used to discount the preserved HTML bodies.

No proposed direct links are activated. FitzRoy incoming letters answer missing Darwin notes or communications; Jenyns outgoing letters answer missing Jenyns notes/letters or external manuscripts; incoming author prose is never treated as Darwin voice or as proof of Darwin receipt.

FitzRoy 386 and 387 are distinct replies: 386 answers a Monday note received the prior evening, while 387 answers a letter written that morning and separately cites the Monday letter. Same preface topic and adjacent dates do not merge them.

Jenyns 596 is a fragment beginning mid-sentence; its surviving Cambridge and Scorpaena material does not uniquely identify a Darwin response. Missing opening/body text must be obtained before stronger attribution or pairing.

For cross-correspondent context, full preserved records DCP-LETT-353, DCP-LETT-361A, DCP-LETT-377A, DCP-LETT-384 and DCP-LETT-388 were read. They clarify publication/prospectus context but do not supply a direct prompt for a batch-05 pair and are not used as relationship proof.

External material still needed for direct pairing includes the missing Darwin notes to FitzRoy, FitzRoy’s long 1840 letter, missing Jenyns fish correspondence and manuscripts/notes, the original preface/prospectus, and the newspaper report behind the 1843 appointment letter.
